title: Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to accelerate drug discovery with AI
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:51 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026

Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to accelerate drug discovery with AI

Isomorphic Labs Ltd. today announced that it has closed a $5 billion investment led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital.

The venture capital firms were joined by more than a half-dozen other backers. The group included Isomorphic parent Alphabet Inc., which made a “significant investment.” The search giant provided the capital through its GV and CapitalG startup funds.

Isomorphic offers a software platform called the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine, or IsoDDE for short. It uses artificial intelligence to speed up several of the tasks involved in developing new medicines. The Alphabet unit says that multiple pharmaceutical companies are already using IsoDDE to power drug discovery programs.

Pathogens such as viruses comprise numerous proteins that each power a different biological process. Drugs work by neutralizing a single, particularly important protein without which the pathogen can’t function. Developing a new drug requires researchers to find a vulnerable protein within a pathogen and then develop a compound that can effectively target it.

The first step of the workflow is mapping out the shape of a target protein. Researchers look for so-called binding pockets, recesses on the protein’s surface to which a drug can be attached. The task is highly complicated because proteins don’t have fixed shapes. Their configuration changes when they interact with other molecules or encounter new environmental conditions, which happens often.

Isomorphic says that IsoDDE speeds up the task of finding binding pockets. When there are no such pockets, it helps researchers develop compounds that cause a target protein to form them.

Once scientists identify a binding pocket, they have to find a way of attaching a drug molecule to it. The pharmaceutical industry searches for such binding mechanisms using a method called FEP. FEP algorithms can be highly hardware-intensive, which makes them costly. Moreover, they often require a detailed, three-dimensional model of a target protein.

The process of creating 3D protein models for FEP algorithms is itself a highly complex task. It requires scientists to freeze a target protein in a crystal and scan it using specialized X-ray equipment.

IsoDDE skips that step of the research workflow. Furthermore, Isomorphic

summary.tldr:
Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs has secured $5 billion in a new funding round led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with additional participation from Alphabet Inc. via its GV and CapitalG funds. The company, led by CEO Demis Hassabis, develops the Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine (IsoDDE), an AI-driven platform designed to accelerate pharmaceutical research by automating complex protein analysis and drug-target identification tasks.

IsoDDE aims to replace traditional, hardware-intensive methods like Free Energy Perturbation (FEP) algorithms, which typically require high-resolution 3D protein models derived from labor-intensive X-ray crystallography. The engine identifies binding pockets on protein surfaces and can induce the formation of such pockets where they do not naturally exist. Isomorphic claims the platform produces higher-quality output than FEP-based workflows with greater speed and precision. The new capital will be used to build bioengineering infrastructure, advance foundational biology models, and move the company's internal therapeutic programs toward clinical trials.
takeaways: **Funding:** Isomorphic Labs raised $5 billion in a round led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, with significant investment from parent company Alphabet.
**Core Technology:** The Isomorphic Labs Drug Design Engine (IsoDDE) automates the identification of protein binding pockets and drug-target compound development.
**Workflow Efficiency:** IsoDDE eliminates the need for X-ray crystallography-based 3D protein modeling, a prerequisite for traditional FEP (Free Energy Perturbation) algorithms.
**Strategic Goals:** The company plans to utilize the funding to scale its partner ecosystem, expand bioengineering infrastructure, and progress internal therapeutic programs to clinical trials.

title: Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
author: Nilay Patel
contentSnippet: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think so,” he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic’s team has “wireheaded” themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn’t quite as firm about it. “It’s a good debate,” he said. “I’m not sort of dogmatic about it. What I’m saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?” I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter’s questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. “Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be,” he said. “But remember, the model has no limits. It’ll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it.” Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. “If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?” he asked. “If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That’s the debate.” “I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one — at least in a democracy — can

summary.tldr:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, speaking at a roundtable following the Microsoft Ignite keynote in San Francisco, articulated a shift in his perspective on Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), focusing on its systemic impact on political economy rather than the technical definition of consciousness. Nadella explicitly rejected the notion that frontier models like Anthropic’s Claude possess consciousness or moral status, aligning with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s stance against granting rights to AI systems. He characterized the current discourse surrounding AI as overly focused on narrow competition between tech firms for market capitalization, arguing instead that the true risk lies in the potential for AI to disrupt the fundamental structure of firms, labor, and democratic governance.

Nadella posited that if intelligence exhibits network effects, the traditional concept of a firm may collapse as human capital is subsumed into 'token capital.' He warned that a monopolistic AI outcome—where a single entity controls the primary intelligence infrastructure—would be incompatible with democratic processes and economic stability. To counter this, Nadella emphasized Microsoft’s strategy of promoting a multi-model ecosystem, allowing enterprise clients to select cost-effective models and maintain data sovereignty. He argued that for a diverse economy to persist, the market must support a wide array of models rather than consolidating power into one or two dominant firms.
takeaways: **AGI Stance:** Satya Nadella defines his 'AGI-pilled' status as a concern for the political economy and the structural organization of society rather than a belief in model consciousness.

**Moral Status:** Nadella and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman oppose granting moral status or rights to AI models, explicitly distancing themselves from the principles held by companies like Anthropic.

**Economic Risk:** Nadella warned that if AI models achieve monopoly status, they could effectively replace traditional firms, potentially leading to the collapse of labor markets and democratic election integrity.

**Strategic Counter-Measure:** Microsoft is positioning its AI platform to support a multi-model, sovereign-data approach to prevent the centralization of intelligence and ensure the survival of a diverse corporate landscape.

title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.

China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks.

Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.

The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”

Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.

Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.

In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.

Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Fe

summary.tldr:
Nvidia has officially ceased the sale of H200 chips to China, marking the end of a controversial export loophole that previously allowed shipments via the U.S. subject to a 25% tariff. This policy shift follows the departure of co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, whose exit was reportedly linked to an affair with the CEO of a firm under investigation for chip smuggling. In response to the evolving regulatory landscape, Nvidia has established a board-level committee dedicated to national security, export compliance, and global trade risk management.

New U.S. export rules, issued Monday, now prohibit the sale of advanced chips to foreign data centers that provide services to Chinese customers. While investment bank Jefferies projected a potential $44 billion to $62 billion hit to Nvidia’s data center revenue, acting CEO Colette Kress stated that high demand for next-generation hardware like the Vera Rubin architecture will offset these losses. The new regulations also threaten Nvidia’s market share in Southeast Asian nations like Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia, as data centers in these regions must now certify they do not serve Chinese clients to remain eligible for Nvidia hardware.
takeaways: **Export Policy Shift:** Nvidia is terminating the sale of H200 chips to China, ending a deal previously brokered by Jensen Huang and Donald Trump that included a 25% U.S. tariff.

**Revenue Impact Forecast:** Jefferies estimates a $44 billion to $62 billion revenue reduction for Nvidia's data center segment, though acting CEO Colette Kress claims the Vera Rubin backlog will neutralize this impact.
**New Regulatory Constraints:** Recent rules bar the export of advanced chips to any foreign data center that provides remote access or services to Chinese customers.
**Compliance Requirements:** Data centers must now provide formal certification that they do not serve Chinese customers to purchase Nvidia hardware, or risk losing access to the company's products.
**Market Exposure:** Critics estimate that up to 20% of Nvidia's revenue is linked to Chinese demand, with the company's Singapore subsidiary reporting $104 billion in annual revenue in 2025.

title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
author: Vinay Arora
contentSnippet: Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo , combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod. How the integration works The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components: HyperPod Inference Operator manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource. Its dynamoSpec section supplies the Dynamo configuration. Dynamo operator manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) , including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements. Grove coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships. Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on. Deployment architecture The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both p

summary.tldr:
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference has integrated NVIDIA Dynamo, an open-source distributed inference framework, to facilitate the deployment of large language models (LLMs) that exceed the memory capacity of single instances. For instance, models like GLM-5.3 with FP8 weights surpass the 640 GB memory limit of an ml.p5.48xlarge instance when accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. The integration leverages HyperPod’s infrastructure—including Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and automated node health monitoring—to support multi-node deployments and disaggregated inference architectures.

The architecture utilizes the HyperPod Inference Operator to manage endpoints via InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) and DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) resources. Key components include the Dynamo operator for managing model workers and replica counts, Grove for coordinating multi-node scaling, and the Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler, which employs gang scheduling to ensure multi-node workers are placed on GPU resources simultaneously. The system supports engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, allowing for disaggregated prefill and decode operations where separate worker pools process prompts and generate tokens independently.
takeaways: **Hardware Constraint:** A single ml.p5.48xlarge instance provides 640 GB of GPU memory, which is insufficient for models like GLM-5.3 in FP8 precision when including KV cache and runtime overhead.
**Architecture Components:** The integration uses the HyperPod Inference Operator, Dynamo operator, Grove for pod coordination, and the KAI Scheduler for gang scheduling.
**Supported Engines:** The Dynamo framework within HyperPod supports vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM for distributed inference.
**Disaggregated Serving:** The system enables independent scaling of prefill workers (prompt processing) and decode workers (token generation) to optimize performance for long prompts.

title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang’s exit
author: Sarah Perez
contentSnippet:
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation.

“At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call.

“Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face.

Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.”

“That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,”

summary.tldr:
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress confirmed that the company’s open-source AI strategy remains unchanged following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang. During the company’s latest earnings call, Kress emphasized a continued commitment to fostering an open model ecosystem, citing a 35-fold year-over-year increase in weekly token volume on OpenRouter. The company’s $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face, which serves 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, remains on track despite the leadership transition.

Kress identified Nemotron as the most widely used U.S.-based open model on OpenRouter. The leadership shift follows Huang’s resignation amid reports of extramarital affairs and an SEC investigation into potential disclosure failures. takeaways: **Acquisition Status:** Nvidia’s $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face is proceeding as planned, marking the second-largest acquisition in the company's history.
**Model Performance:** The Nemotron model family is currently the most widely used U.S. open model on the OpenRouter platform.
**Market Growth:** Weekly token volume on OpenRouter has seen a 35-fold year-over-year increase, with a 3.5-fold growth observed in the last three months alone.
**Hugging Face Scale:** The platform currently supports 18 million developers and 200,000 corporate entities.

title: External sandboxes for coding agents
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi

summary.tldr:
Researchers at Prime Radiant have introduced the 'external sandbox' pattern, a security architecture designed to isolate code execution for AI coding agents. By decoupling the agent from the execution environment, this pattern mitigates risks such as prompt injection or accidental system damage when running local models. The project provides a standardized localhost API, allowing developers to integrate sandboxing with existing tools like Pi, Claude Code, and Codex.

The initiative includes three distinct sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86, which utilizes v86 to run Alpine Linux via WebAssembly; external-sandbox-container, which leverages Apple Containers to run Alpine Linux; and external-sandbox-quicksand, which uses Microsoft’s Quicksand library to bundle QEMU and Alpine Linux within a Python package. Each implementation features an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy for network traffic control and a credential replacement mechanism that enables authenticated API calls without exposing secrets directly to the agent.
takeaways: **Sandbox Implementations:** Three distinct versions are available: v86 (WebAssembly-based), container (Apple Containers-based), and quicksand (QEMU-based).
**Network Security:** Each sandbox includes an optional HTTP/HTTPS proxy to restrict agent-executed code to specific, pre-approved hosts.
**Credential Management:** The architecture supports a credential replacement mechanism, allowing agents to perform authenticated API requests without direct access to sensitive secrets.
**Compatibility:** The standardized localhost API allows for immediate integration with existing coding agents including Pi, Claude Code, and Codex.

title: Perplexity Computer Adds Multiagent: Up to 16 AI Agents That Cross-Check Work
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Perplexity has added Multiagent to Computer , its agent platform for research and multistep work. Perplexity Computer Multiagent is a new effort level that sits above Ultra. A lead agent runs a team of agents on different frontier models. Those agents work in parallel, share findings directly and check each other’s work. For developers and analysts, the change is structural. Supporting agents no longer report only to a single lead. TL;DR Size: Up to 16 agents per task, plus the lead. Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: Perplexity’s cloud. Web only, Perplexity Max plan. No local or quantized option. Performance: Not benchmarked. Perplexity published no accuracy or speed numbers. Best: 16-agent cap with direct agent-to-agent checks across 3 default model families (Claude, GPT, Gemini). What is Perplexity Computer Multiagent? Multiagent is the highest effort level in Perplexity Computer. It coordinates AI models to analyze complex tasks and cross-check their work, per Perplexity’s announcement . It builds on effort controls launched on September 17, 2026 . That release added 4 settings: Light, Standard, High and Ultra. Each setting picks the orchestrator model and its reasoning depth. Lower settings use less expensive models. How does Multiagent work? The lead agent plans the task and assigns parts to supporting agents. It can assign up to 16 agents and also does part of the work itself. In Perplexity’s example, Claude Fable 5.2 plans the task. It splits work among agents running Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Carbon. Those 3 models form the default team. Fable 5.2 and GPT 6 Astra join as supporting agents only when requested or needed. Key mechanics from the launch post : Direct sharing: Agents use evidence found by others, question assumptions and flag discrepancies. Shared files: Agents coordinate edits to shared files. One agent can update revenue assumptions and notify another to reuse them in a valuation. Single point of contact: Users talk only to the lead. The lead merges findings into one response. Follow-ups: The lead tells affected agents what changed. The team continues its existing work. Control: Users see which agents and models are running. Stopping the thread stops the whole team. Model choice: Users can name specific models in their query. Multiagent vs Ultra vs Model Council Perplexity now offers 3 ways to put several models on

summary.tldr:
Perplexity has introduced 'Multiagent' to its Computer platform, a new high-effort tier that allows a lead agent to orchestrate up to 16 supporting AI agents to execute complex, multistep research tasks. Positioned above the existing 'Ultra' effort level, this system enables parallel processing where agents share findings, cross-check work, and coordinate edits on shared files. The lead agent manages the task lifecycle, merging outputs into a single response for the user while maintaining a single point of contact for follow-up queries.

The architecture relies on a default team composed of Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon, with Claude Fable 5.2 typically serving as the lead orchestrator. Depending on task requirements, additional models like GPT 6 Astra may be dynamically invoked. The system supports direct agent-to-agent communication, allowing one agent to flag discrepancies in another's work or update shared data, such as revenue assumptions, in real-time. Users retain visibility into which models are active and can specify preferred models within their queries.

Multiagent is currently available exclusively via the web-based Perplexity Max plan and operates entirely within Perplexity’s cloud infrastructure, with no local or quantized deployment options provided. Perplexity has not released specific benchmark data, accuracy metrics, or speed comparisons for this multi-agent configuration. The feature builds upon the effort-control framework launched on September 17, 2026, which previously included Light, Standard, High, and Ultra settings.
takeaways: **Agent Capacity:** The system supports a lead agent plus up to 16 supporting agents per task.
**Default Model Stack:** The default team utilizes Claude Opus 5.5, GPT 6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Carbon, orchestrated by Claude Fable 5.2.
**Operational Mechanics:** Agents perform direct cross-checking, share findings, and coordinate edits on common files, with the lead agent responsible for merging final outputs.
**Availability:** The feature is restricted to the web-based Perplexity Max plan with no local execution or model quantization options.
**Control Interface:** Users can view active agents and models in real-time and terminate the entire multi-agent thread via a single stop command.

title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
author: Pallav Gupta
contentSnippet: As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload. Solution overview Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow: Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph , an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock Ag

summary.tldr:
Flightscape, an airline operations platform, has implemented three optimization strategies for its Amazon Bedrock-based Training Schedule Optimization agent to address high token consumption and latency when processing 20 MB+ JSON payloads. The agent, which manages crew training schedules using over 40 tools, initially suffered from request latencies exceeding 15 seconds due to the redundant injection of full JSON payloads into the LLM context window during every tool invocation. This architectural bottleneck caused context window exhaustion and significant cost inflation during multi-turn conversations.

By re-engineering the data flow within their LangGraph-based architecture, the team achieved a 71% reduction in token consumption and an 80% decrease in average latency on a 23 MB benchmark payload. The system architecture involves an Optimizer generating a response, a Business Rules Validator creating a validation report, and an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for querying these outputs. These optimizations allow the agent to maintain full reasoning capabilities while handling large-scale structured data inputs within the constraints of Amazon Bedrock's production environment.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** Implementation of optimization strategies resulted in a 71% reduction in token consumption and an 80% reduction in average latency.
**Baseline Metrics:** The unoptimized agent experienced average request latencies exceeding 15 seconds when processing multi-megabyte JSON payloads.

**System Architecture:** The agent utilizes LangGraph for orchestration and runs on Amazon Bedrock, managing a workflow that includes an Optimizer, a Business Rules Validator, and a conversational AI interface.
**Scale:** The agent is designed to handle complex queries across 40+ tools and JSON payloads exceeding 20 MB in size.

title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back.

During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering.

“On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China , and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security.

The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia . Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress , who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the company was looking at both internal and external candidates.

title: OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday work
author: Duncan Riley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 17:39 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026

OpenAI rolls out GPT-6.2 Astra for professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday work

OpenAI Group PBC today announced the launch of GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier artificial intelligence model for complex professional work that is claimed to outperform its predecessor at less than a third of the cost, along with an updated version of its everyday model, GPT-6.2 Sol.

The new models are aimed at businesses and developers looking for frontier performance at a cost that works at scale, with both said to deliver better results on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens.

According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new high on Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multistep professional work, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra while costing under a third as much. It is claimed to have finished 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

OpenAI is positioning GPT-6.2 Astra as the best model in the world for scientists, with the model scoring 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a benchmark for scientific work carried out in a terminal. On Harvey LAB-AA, a test of legal assignments, the model more than doubled the pass rate of Fable 5.2 at about one-sixth of the cost.

Along with improved benchmark scores, GPT-6.2 Astra was trained to create slides, spreadsheets and documents that more closely follow the conventions used by professionals in fields such as law, sales, finance and accounting. The model can match a slide template from an original file or a screenshot, including layout, colors and typography down to the exact font size.

Early testers of the model include accounting AI startup Basis, which said that its average time for long-horizon accounting work fell by 50%, with the time for its most complex work falling by up to 73%.

Described by OpenAI as its go-to model for everyday work, GPT-6.2 Sol is claimed to let users complete more tasks on the same paid plan than GPT-6.1 Sol did. According to OpenAI, the model came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI Inc.’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at about one-fifth of the cost.

GPT-6.2 Astra comes less than two months after OpenAI called off the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after internal testing found the model fell short on staying within scope and aut

OpenAI Group PBC announced the release of GPT-6.2 Astra, a frontier AI model targeting complex professional work, alongside GPT-6.2 Sol, an updated everyday model. OpenAI claims GPT-6.2 Astra outperforms its predecessor at less than a third of the cost while using fewer output tokens, following the cancellation of a planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra due to scope and authorization issues.

GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Agents' Last Exam at under a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 5% of its cost. For scientific work, it scored 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, and on Harvey LAB-AA for legal assignments, it more than doubled Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth of the cost. Meanwhile, GPT-6.2 Sol scored within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI's FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at about one-fifth of the cost. GPT-6.2 Astra also meets OpenAI's 'High' threshold for AI self-improvement and the 'Critical' cybersecurity threshold, prompting tighter safeguards.

Both models are available to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users via ChatGPT Work and Codex, and to developers through the OpenAI API. API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is set at $8 per million input tokens, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 per million output tokens (a 20% discount from GPT-6 Astra), while GPT-6.2 Sol maintains pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
takeaways: **Performance and Benchmarks:** GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher on Agents' Last Exam than GPT-6 Astra, 9 percentage points higher on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, and more than doubled Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate on Harvey LAB-AA.
**Coding Benchmark:** GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra on Cognition AI Inc.'s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark while costing about one-fifth as much.

**Safety and Governance:** GPT-6.2 Astra is the first externally released OpenAI model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement and meets the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework.

**API Pricing:** GPT-6.2 Astra API pricing is $8 per million input tokens ($0.40 cached) and $40 per million output tokens. GPT-6.2 Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
**Product Availability:** Both models are available starting today for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, as well as via the OpenAI API.

title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
author: Meghan Kothari
contentSnippet: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock . Why unneeded model calls add up The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost. At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways: Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps. Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds. Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower. Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked. Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens , often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all? How to decide whether a step needs a model Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements: Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first. Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema? Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no? If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model. title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
author: Dmitry Soldatkin
contentSnippet: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. title: Clearing Up the Confusion on AI Data Retention: Two Standard Designs Explained
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Data retention has become one of the most misunderstood terms in AI infrastructure. After a wave of AI security headlines, many dev teams now ask a simple question. Does my AI provider keep my data? The honest answer depends on how you send it. Send a prompt to an inference API, and it is processed and returned without being kept. That design is called zero data retention (ZDR). Upload a dataset for a batch job, and it stays stored until you delete it. Both are standard designs, and in both the customer is in control. What changes is who manages the data lifecycle, and where. Fireworks AI cofounder and CEO Lin Qiao set out a clear way to think about this. In a November 13, 2026 post on X , she described two standard API designs. Each one decides where control of the data lifecycle sits. The same split has shaped data processing systems for decades. In this article, we will go through that framework with examples from public API documentation. TL;DR The framework: Two standard API designs : upload, use, delete, or send, compute, return. What it is: ZDR is a per-endpoint commitment not to persist covered prompts and outputs after an eligible request. Where it applies: Eligibility depends on the endpoint, request flags and account settings, not the vendor name. Stored features: Batch, file and dataset features keep data until it is deleted or expires. Bottom line: Prefer ephemeral endpoints. If you upload, deletion is your job, so never assume an expiry. What is an AI data retention policy? An AI data retention policy defines what a platform stores from your requests, and for how long. OpenAI’s data controls describe two layers. Application state is data a feature must keep, such as uploaded files. Abuse-monitoring logs are copies held for safety review. A platform can be at zero on one layer and not the other. What are the two common API designs? AI inference and training APIs follow two lifecycle designs. The difference is who manages the data, and where. Pattern 1: Customer-managed retention (upload, use, delete) You create a file or dataset, run jobs against it, then delete it. The platform keeps the data stored and available until you ask for deletion. It cannot know when you are finished unless you define it. So deletion is your job, done through the platform’s APIs. Batch APIs with uploaded datasets are the standard example: OpenAI Batch : upload a JSONL

The honest answer depends on how you send it. Send a prompt to an inference API, and it is processed and returned without being kept. That design is called zero data retention (ZDR).
takeaways: Upload a dataset for a batch job, and it stays stored until you delete it.
Both are standard designs, and in both the customer is in control.

title: Idle, then spiking: Why AI agents are breaking Kubernetes resource planning
author: Jonathan Anthony
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 15:35 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026

Idle, then spiking: Why AI agents are breaking Kubernetes resource planning

AI agents are changing the economics of cloud infrastructure, and autonomous orchestration is becoming the way platform teams keep up. Agentic workloads sit idle and then spike without warning. That pattern leaves static resource settings either wasteful or likely to fail.

Container orchestration for AI is fast becoming the backbone of production AI, and agents are adding a new layer of strain. Compute costs are climbing and reliability problems are harder to contain because everything an agent does ultimately runs on CPU and memory, according to Yodar Shafrir (pictured), founder and chief executive officer of ScaleOps Inc.

“Agents and all the agent workloads pretty much made everything way more complex when managing infrastructure,” Shafrir said. “Eventually, all the complexity that existed before just got much worse. Today, the compute cost has grown dramatically. Everything that agents execute eventually runs on compute.”

Shafrir spoke with theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how autonomous orchestration lets ScaleOps adjust resources in real time as AI agents spike, cutting both costs and crashes. (* Disclosure below.)

Why autonomous orchestration fits the agentic era

Agents behave differently from traditional microservices. An agent waits for a human or another agent, checks with a large language model and then runs its task in a burst. Teams must provision for the highest spike while the agent holds its memory the whole time, Shafrir explained. When resources fall short, a crashed step has to rerun and burns tokens all over again.

“We actually see that agents crash due to not having enough resources 80% more often compared with traditional microservices,” Shafrir said. “The reliability is much harder to manage.”

For ScaleOps, the answer is to make resource decisions in real time. It adjusts allocations, replicas and node placement for every application, agent and Model Context Protocol server, which the company says cuts cloud costs by 70% to 80%. Customers such as Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc. build trust by first running the platform in read-only mode on their hardest environments,

summary.tldr:
ScaleOps Inc. CEO Yodar Shafrir reports that AI agent workloads are destabilizing traditional Kubernetes resource planning due to their 'idle-then-spike' execution patterns. Unlike standard microservices, agents remain idle while awaiting LLM responses or human input, then trigger sudden, high-intensity compute bursts. This behavior forces static provisioning to either over-allocate resources—leading to significant waste—or under-allocate, resulting in frequent crashes that necessitate costly token re-runs. Shafrir notes that agents experience resource-related crashes 80% more frequently than traditional microservices.

To address this, ScaleOps provides an autonomous orchestration platform that dynamically adjusts allocations, replicas, and node placement in real-time. By analyzing historical patterns and application dependencies, the platform enables memory swapping and allows secondary workloads to utilize resources during an agent's idle periods. ScaleOps claims this approach improves cost efficiency for agentic workloads by up to 90% and reduces overall cloud infrastructure costs by 70% to 80%. Major enterprise customers, including Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc., utilize the platform, often beginning with a read-only mode to validate resource decisions before full implementation.
takeaways: **Reliability Gap:** AI agents crash due to insufficient resource allocation 80% more often than traditional microservices.
**Cost Efficiency:** ScaleOps claims its autonomous orchestration platform improves agentic workload cost efficiency by 90% and reduces total cloud spend by 70% to 80%.
**Technical Mechanism:** The platform utilizes real-time memory swapping and dynamic resource reallocation to allow non-agent workloads to consume idle capacity reserved for agents.
**Enterprise Adoption:** Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc. are identified as customers utilizing the ScaleOps platform for managing complex, agent-heavy environments.

title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
author: Sana Iqbal
contentSnippet: As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record. Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet. In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types. How custom metadata works With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema : field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the

summary.tldr:
AWS has introduced custom metadata schemas for the AWS Agent Registry, enabling organizations to enforce standardized key-value pairs across their agentic fleet. This feature allows administrators to define specific attributes—such as business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments—that must be included when publishing agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, or skills. By establishing a unified vocabulary, the registry ensures that all records carry consistent, organization-specific facts, facilitating better governance and discovery.

When an administrator defines a schema, they specify field names, data types, allowed values, and requirement status (required vs. optional). The AWS Agent Registry enforces these constraints during the record submission process, validating that all publishers adhere to the defined schema. This structured metadata allows approvers to review records against standardized criteria and enables both human users and automated agents to filter and discover resources based on these validated attributes, creating a centralized source of truth for an organization's agentic infrastructure.
takeaways: **Schema Enforcement:** Administrators define custom metadata schemas that mandate specific key-value pairs for all records within an AWS Agent Registry.
**Validation Workflow:** The registry automatically validates submitted records against the defined schema, ensuring field names, types, and allowed values are consistent across the organization.
**Discovery Utility:** Standardized metadata allows for improved filtering and discovery of agents, MCP servers, and skills by both human users and automated agents.
**Governance Scope:** The feature supports tracking organizational-specific attributes such as risk classifications, resource ownership, and deployment environments.

title: Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab
author: Zeus Kerravala
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 15:27 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026

Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab

For most of its history, the high-performance computing market measured progress the same way: how fast a machine could solve a fixed problem. Rankings rose, a new system took the top spot, and the cycle started over. Raw performance remains the foundation of scientific computing, and Nvidia Corp. brought plenty of it to SC26.

But this week, Nvidia argued that speed at solving a single problem is no longer the right way to measure leadership. An equally important question now is how many times a researcher can go from hypothesis to result in a day, and what happens when the “researcher” is an artificial intelligence agent that never sleeps.

That idea ties together Nvidia’s bevy of announcements at the show. The company introduced open science models, a CPU-only supercomputing rack, a new HPC-specific GPU, a batch of CUDA-X libraries, quantum integration for the Slurm workload manager, a quantum co-design platform with IBM and Fermilab, and a co-packaged optics deployment at Lambda. It also marked CUDA’s 20th birthday.

Taken individually, these announcements look like a typical supercomputing show news payload. Taken together, they describe a stack built for a different user, namely the AI agent that reasons through a scientific problem, calls a simulation, reads the result and decides what to try next.

Ian Buck (pictured), Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, summed up this thesis when introducing Rubin HPC: “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery.” This marks an important industry shift. Simulation used to be the end product. In an agentic workflow, it’s a tool call within a much larger loop of hypothesis, simulation, and refinement.

When an agent can generate thousands of candidate molecules or material designs, the bottleneck shifts from ideas to the time required to test them. That’s why so much of the SC26 news focuses on loop speed alongside peak flops. Nvidia says cuPhoton cut the time to correlate Event Horizon Telescope black-hole data from more than a month to eight minutes.

At Pacific Fusion, a Nemotron-powered agent running on the same system can analyze plasma simulations as they run, allowing researchers to steer the simulation in real time rather than wai

summary.tldr:
At SC26, Nvidia shifted its high-performance computing (HPC) strategy from raw peak-performance metrics to 'time-to-insight' for autonomous AI agents. The company introduced a comprehensive stack—including the Rubin HPC GPU, the Vera CPU, and expanded CUDA-X libraries—designed to support agentic workflows where AI models iteratively hypothesize, simulate, and refine scientific results. By optimizing for loop speed rather than single-job completion, Nvidia aims to reduce the latency between scientific questions and actionable data, exemplified by cuPhoton reducing black-hole data correlation time from over a month to eight minutes.

Nvidia is aggressively targeting the CPU-bound HPC market with its Vera processor, which the company claims delivers 1.9x the performance and 2.4x the performance-per-watt of x86 alternatives on OpenFOAM simulations. To ensure seamless integration, Nvidia is extending the Slurm workload manager to orchestrate heterogeneous environments, including CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processors (QPUs). This orchestration layer is supported by major quantum players like IBM, Alice & Bob, and Quantinuum, positioning Nvidia as the central coordinator for scientific computing regardless of the underlying hardware architecture.

Domain-specific model tuning emerged as a critical theme, with Nvidia highlighting that post-trained, specialized models like Nemotron 3.5 Super VL often outperform general-purpose frontier models in accuracy and cost-efficiency for scientific tasks. Furthermore, Nvidia is addressing infrastructure bottlenecks through co-packaged optics, which Lambda reported provides 5x better power efficiency and 15x higher reliability than traditional pluggable optics, a necessary evolution for the continuous, high-uptime requirements of agentic scientific research.
takeaways: **Vera CPU Performance:** Nvidia’s Vera CPU demonstrated 1.9x higher performance and 2.4x better performance-per-watt compared to x86 architectures in OpenFOAM airflow simulations.
**Nemotron Specialization:** Post-trained Nemotron models achieved 61% accuracy in quantum-dot synthesis, outperforming GPT-6 Astra (54%) at 10–20x lower inference costs.
**Quantum Decoding:** The TCBP-JOBS decoder in CUDA-Q QEC 0.9.0 accelerates error-correction research by up to 13,000x, reducing specific design study times from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

**Co-packaged Optics:** Lambda’s deployment of co-packaged optics reduced network latency by up to 10% at pod scale and maintained a median operating temperature of 36°C, compared to 51°C for pluggable optics.

**Slurm Quantum Integration:** Over 30 data centers are deploying more than 50 quantum processors using Nvidia’s expanded Slurm scheduler, which now supports unified orchestration of QPUs, CPUs, and GPUs.

title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Nithyashree Alwarsamy
contentSnippet: Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario. Solution overview Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the toke

summary.tldr:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore has introduced new OAuth integration patterns for connecting AI agents to Snowflake Cortex via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The architecture utilizes the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway to aggregate Snowflake-managed MCP tools—specifically Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst—into a unified catalog for agent consumption. The integration relies on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, which functions as a credential broker to manage outbound authentication between the Gateway and the Snowflake-managed MCP server.

The technical implementation focuses on three primary OAuth configurations: Snowflake-native OAuth (per-user without an external IdP), three-legged OAuth utilizing a third-party corporate SSO, and two-legged OAuth using a shared service user. Additionally, the system supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant via the TOKEN_EXCHANGE mechanism, enabling per-user identity propagation for unattended workloads without requiring manual consent prompts. The Gateway facilitates this by obtaining a workload token via GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and subsequently calling GetResourceOauth2Token to secure the connection to the Snowflake-managed MCP server.
takeaways: **Architecture Components:** The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for tool aggregation and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity as the centralized credential broker.
**Supported Tools:** The Snowflake-managed MCP server exposes Snowflake Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as discoverable tools for MCP-aware clients.
**Authentication Workflow:** The Gateway authenticates inbound via JWT and outbound via OAuth2 tokens retrieved through the GetResourceOauth2Token API call.
**Identity Propagation:** The system supports TOKEN_EXCHANGE (OBO grant) to maintain per-user identity context for unattended agent workloads.

title: Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement
author: Kyt Dotson
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 15:05 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026

Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement

Microsoft Corp. today rolled out new generative artificial intelligence models and updates to Foundry, the company’s unified enterprise platform that helps developers and organizations ground, test and deploy AI applications and autonomous agents.

Updates to Foundry IQ , part of Microsoft IQ , now provide an enterprise knowledge graph out of the box, delivering a full estate of unstructured and application data to provide rich context for building applications and delivering on essential use cases.

Microsoft also said Foundry now uses existing transparency and observability capabilities to help customers create learning loops. Internal evaluations allow autonomous agents to establish baselines for quality, safety, latency and cost, enabling continuous behavioral improvements.

This includes human annotations, now in preview, that allow experts to rate and comment on agent traces based on business judgment. It feeds back into an improvement loop. It’s combined with optimization tests against evaluations and comparisons against real-world results. Foundry now also has new capabilities to adapt to supported models with organizational data to apply reinforcement learning while Foundry runs compute.

Each improvement becomes the next baseline and teams can continue measuring results and test changes, allowing them to improve quality.

Microsoft’s updated decision model and first-party AI models

Microsoft today announced Decision-1.1 is generally available. It’s a fast, cost-effective model designed to make reliable decisions in software at scale.

The generative AI model can make decisions dynamically at low cost, rather than relying on hard-coded rules, while offering superior decision-making capabilities compared with large language models. LLMs spend a lot of time making decisions in routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control by “thinking it through,” which is unnecessary. Decision models are designed to reach answers quickly within constrained definitions and provide calibrated confidence scores, allowing applications to defer when uncertainty is high.

The new model builds on the previous generation, Microsoft-Decision-1, released in October. The new model delivers a significant improvement in i

summary.tldr:
Microsoft has expanded its Foundry enterprise AI platform with new first-party models and enhanced agentic continuous improvement workflows. The update introduces Foundry IQ, which provides an out-of-the-box enterprise knowledge graph to ground AI applications in unstructured and application data. The platform now incorporates human-in-the-loop annotations, allowing experts to rate agent traces, which feeds into a reinforcement learning loop that optimizes agents against quality, safety, latency, and cost baselines.

Key model releases include Decision-1.1, a specialized model for dynamic software decision-making built on Google’s Gemma 4 26B A4 architecture. Unlike general-purpose LLMs, Decision-1.1 is optimized for routing, classification, and workflow control, providing calibrated confidence scores to handle uncertainty. Additionally, Microsoft expanded its MAI first-party model family: MAI-Code-2 and MAI-Code-2-Flash (coding), MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash (multimodal editing), and MAI-Cyber-2-Flash (cybersecurity). These models are integrated into Foundry, which now supports a model router, an AI Gateway, and a library of over 11,000 models from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Mistral.
takeaways: **Decision-1.1 Architecture:** Built on Google’s Gemma 4 26B A4 base, featuring multimodal support for image analysis in instructions.
**Foundry Model Ecosystem:** The platform now hosts over 11,000 models and includes a model router and AI Gateway for intelligent selection.
**Agentic Improvement Loop:** Foundry now supports human annotations for agent traces, enabling reinforcement learning and continuous behavioral refinement against quality and cost metrics.
**MAI Model Availability:** MAI-Code-2 is generally available on GitHub; MAI-Code-2-Flash is in private preview in Foundry; MAI-Image-2.7 series and MAI-Cyber-2-Flash are currently in preview.

title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
author: Varun Rajan
contentSnippet: Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference. In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models. Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change. Prepare data without hand-building pipelines With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want. Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. You describe the task in a short labeling spec, which is validated against your own examples before the full dataset is labeled. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, such as classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score. Human review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced new AI data preparation capabilities within Amazon SageMaker, designed to streamline the creation of high-quality training and evaluation datasets for generative AI and machine learning workflows. The suite allows developers to generate synthetic data, assess existing datasets, and integrate human-in-the-loop feedback directly through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. By providing modular building blocks, the service aims to reduce the time data scientists spend on manual pipeline construction, data wrangling, and formatting tasks.

The platform features an auto-labeling capability that supports classification, named entity recognition (NER), extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, alongside support for custom task definitions. The system utilizes a 'jury' of multiple models to label data; for tasks with fixed answer sets, the level of agreement between these models generates a confidence score for each row. Data rows falling below a user-defined confidence threshold are automatically routed for human review, ensuring quality control before training begins.
takeaways: **Supported Task Types:** Includes classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization.
**Confidence Scoring:** Employs a multi-model 'jury' system to label data, where inter-model agreement determines the confidence score per row.
**Integration Methods:** Capabilities are accessible via Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill within existing notebook or IDE environments.
**Human-in-the-loop:** Automatically routes data rows that fail to meet user-defined confidence thresholds to human reviewers.

title: Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work
author: Marina Temkin
contentSnippet: Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors. Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022. Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis. Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April. Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results.
