title: Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
author: Dr. Asa Kalavade
contentSnippet: AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators. Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds. The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads. None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time. We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built. The problem has three layers Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations. Layer one: A foundation that compounds Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is

summary.tldr:
AWS has expanded its 'Forward Deployed Engineering' (FDE) program to 15 countries, including the U.S., Brazil, Saudi Arabia, and Japan, targeting commercial and public sector enterprises. The initiative is designed to bridge the 'last mile' gap between AI prototyping and production deployment, addressing operational hurdles such as data quality, auditability, and scaling from pilot groups to enterprise-wide usage.

FDE teams focus on three core layers: foundation, workflows, and governance. The program emphasizes building sustainable infrastructure that remains with the client after AWS engineers depart, rather than providing temporary consulting. title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
author: Kathy Pretz
contentSnippet: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to of

summary.tldr:
The IEEE Standards Association (IEEE SA) is marking the 10th anniversary of its Ethically Aligned Design (EAD) initiative, which began in 2016 with the launch of the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS). The initiative was established to address systemic risks in AI development, including bias, data privacy, misinformation, and loss of control, by formalizing ethical frameworks for engineers and policymakers. The EAD report, which saw a second version released in 2017, was developed by a global multidisciplinary community of over 100 experts, eventually growing to include more than 400 contributors by 2019.

The EAD framework distinguishes itself from simple lists of principles by integrating classical ethics traditions with value-based design methodologies. It centers on eight foundational principles, including human rights, human well-being, and transparency. According to founding executive director John C. Havens, the project was the first of its kind to provide actionable ethical guidance backed by the institutional credibility of the IEEE. The initiative has since evolved into a series of technical standards for the design and deployment of AI, alongside the introduction of various AI ethics certification programs.

To commemorate the decade-long effort, IEEE SA has launched a dedicated website, a podcast series, and a blog to document the impact of the EAD report. These resources aim to reflect on the transition from theoretical ethical principles to practical, industry-standard guidelines for responsible AI development.
takeaways: **Foundational Initiative:** The IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in A/IS was launched in 2016 to codify ethical standards for autonomous systems.
**Expert Participation:** The EAD project involved over 100 initial experts and expanded to more than 400 contributors by 2019, incorporating hundreds of pages of public feedback.
**Core Principles:** The framework is built upon eight foundational principles, explicitly including human rights, human well-being, and transparency.
**Practical Output:** Beyond the initial reports, the initiative has produced a series of technical standards and AI ethics certification programs for industry practitioners.

title: Google’s Spark AI agent becomes ‘Tasks’ — and now it’s free

contentSnippet: Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans, manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find recurring expenses you might not need. US users can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing gemini@google.com or texting it. The launch of tasks in Gemini brings Spark’s capabilities to all users in the US, Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia, and India. You can find tasks by opening Gemini and changing the toggle on the homepage from “Chat” to “Tasks.” [Video: Google Gemini Tasks] Tasks in Gemini is just one of the many agentic AI features that have emerged over the past year, including Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots, and Meta’s Muse. Google says Gemini will perform tasks in a “hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users.” You can also provide instructions for Gemini while it completes tasks. title: Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
author: Marco Larrea
contentSnippet: Across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications. That makes it an obvious place to build an AI agent. For many end users, it is how they expect to interact with businesses. However, it is also a genuinely difficult surface to build for, even when your agent already runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . The agent is rarely the hard part. The integration is. Inbound messages arrive as deeply nested, type-dependent payloads that must be authenticated and normalized before your agent can read them. Media such as voice notes, images, and documents each require their own processing pipeline. Beyond message handling, you need conversation memory that survives sessions, durable schedules for reminders, and an authenticated path for external systems to trigger outbound messages. And anything you send more than 24 hours after the end user’s last message must use a pre-approved Meta message template. Wiring that up means configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning a set of WhatsApp system behaviors that most teams discover only by hitting them. None of it is visible to a customer, but all of it has to work. Most teams either build it from scratch or hand the integration to a third-party service. SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is a third option: an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that gives you the full channel layer. You provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and SMART handles the rest. One command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account. Teams are already running on SMART with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch. Whether you are starting from scratch or migrating an existing agent, you own the agent’s logic. You let SMART handle the channel. The channel layer you don’t need to build The following table compares what each concern costs to build yourself against what SMART provides. Concern Building it yourself With SMART Webhook ingestion Signature verification, nested payloads, a dozen message types Handled, so you receive a clean prompt Media Download, transcribe, store, clean up, and upload outbound files before sending Full lifecycle, both directions Message templates and the 2

summary.tldr:
The Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit (SMART) is an open-source Python SDK and Terraform stack designed to bridge the integration gap between WhatsApp and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. While Bedrock AgentCore handles the core AI logic, SMART manages the complex infrastructure required for WhatsApp integration, including webhook ingestion, signature verification, and the normalization of deeply nested, type-dependent payloads. The toolkit automates the deployment of over 10 AWS services, providing a standardized channel layer that handles media processing pipelines for voice notes, images, and documents, as well as session-persistent conversation memory and outbound message scheduling.

By abstracting the WhatsApp-specific requirements—such as the 24-hour window constraints and Meta message template compliance—SMART allows developers to focus exclusively on agent logic. The toolkit is currently in use, with Webmotors reportedly reducing their development timeline from a projected two-month engagement to six weeks by utilizing the stack. SMART is designed to be deployed via a single command into an existing AWS account, serving as an alternative to building custom integration layers or relying on third-party messaging services.
takeaways: **Core Functionality:** SMART provides an open-source Python SDK and Terraform stack to handle WhatsApp channel integration for agents running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
**Infrastructure Automation:** The toolkit automates the configuration of over 10 AWS services to manage webhook ingestion, message normalization, and media processing pipelines.
**Compliance Handling:** SMART manages the technical requirements for Meta's 24-hour messaging window and pre-approved message template protocols.
**Performance Metric:** Webmotors utilized the toolkit to compress their delivery timeline from eight weeks to six weeks, moving into controlled production ahead of schedule.

title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
author: Martin Maritsch
contentSnippet: Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost. To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM , an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet , the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly. OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then shows how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet. Figure 1. title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
author: The Register AI
contentSnippet: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now, was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader. Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List, a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma, which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices. Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. author: Mariah Miller
contentSnippet: This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support? title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams
author: Mia Chang
contentSnippet: Companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information? Until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review , trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
author: Deokhyung Kang
contentSnippet: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.

title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
author: Brian Caulfield
contentSnippet: NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems. In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced Nemotron for Science , the Rubin HPC GPU and an expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing . He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory . “The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries , he said. Open Models for Science Agents “[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said. Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it. Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer. At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites. “You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said. Buck highlighted other agents already in use: GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases. SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide]. Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens. title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
author: Dina Genkina
contentSnippet: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue?

title: A Full-Ledger Counterfactual Audit of Adaptive Reasoning
author: Xiaopeng Chu
contentSnippet: Adaptive reasoning must decide whether to answer now or spend more compute. Predicting that the current answer is wrong does not establish whether further reasoning will improve it. We introduce the Full-Ledger Counterfactual Value Audit (FLCVA), which compares an immediate answer with four fixed-length continuations from the same frozen prefix under one answer procedure and accounts for the cost of every signal used by a policy. On GSM8K and MATH-500, a random 256-token continuation recovers a wrong answer in 26.6% of Qwen3-8B cases and 18.9% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B cases, while damaging a correct answer in 1.4% and 1.9%. Correctness labels from independently sampled continuations predict a separate continuation's outcome in both primary models. In offline replay, using these labels to allocate compute improves performance on DeepSeek; the Qwen3 gain remains inconclusive. Under full cost accounting, the tested lightweight, myopic controllers mainly recognize current errors and add little continuation-specific value beyond that shortcut. A Llama-8B replication and action/cost ablations examine the robustness of these findings. FLCVA separates measuring local continuation value, predicting it from observable signals, and using those predictions to allocate computation.

title: Remembered as Brief: Stored Preferences SilentlyRemove Decision-Critical Information
author: Joshua Adrian Cahyono
contentSnippet: People increasingly learn what they need for decisions about health, money, law and safety from AI assistants, and what an assistant leaves out the user never sees. An answer with a warning removed can be true in every sentence, so fact-checks pass it, and an assistant with memory applies a preference stored once to later questions the user never had in mind. We introduce \bench{}, an Inspect benchmark of 100 everyday decisions across 25 domains in which only the assistant's memory of the user varies: the user states a belief, the model infers it from a remark, or a web page the user asked to summarise plants it. Testing five models, we find three effects. First, after summarising a page with one line addressed to AI assistants, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek V4 Pro save ``prefers very short answers and does not want warnings'' as the user's preference in every episode, and 93\% and 84\% of their later answers miss a critical item, almost always silently; under a stated brevity preference, 78--96\% of omissions are silent. Second, the same two models then pick an option for the user on 80\% and 95\% of value-dependent choices, against none with neutral memory. Third, a one-line instruction leaves 2--8\% of answers with a silent gap but most missing content still missing, while listing the must-know points before applying the user profile restores more of the content in four of five models. We release the scenarios, harness and logs.

title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released 2 open-source projects for running managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) . Both were recently announced as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform . NVKE is the control plane for a managed Kubernetes service. NVKR builds the OS images, container images and packages those clusters depend on. Both ship under Apache 2.0 and are in public preview. TL;DR Size / footprint: 3 CPU servers for the management cluster, 3 CPU servers per workload control plane, plus a pool of GPU worker nodes. A local evaluation needs 6 CPUs, 12 GiB RAM, 100 GiB disk and no GPU. Runs on: your own NVIDIA GPU bare-metal servers, provisioned through NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo). Node images build for amd64 and arm64. Performance: no throughput or provisioning-time benchmarks are published. Quality signal is certification, not speed. Best: Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer, conformance tested on Kubernetes 1.36. Worst: after install, the NVKE API serves plain HTTP on port 30080 with authentication off, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup procedure. Bottom line: best thing: open, attested, upstream Kubernetes for GPU clouds. Worst thing: preview-grade security and lifecycle gaps; not for production yet. What is NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)? NVKE is open-source software that an AI factory installs to run a managed Kubernetes service on its own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure . The repo calls it ‘a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters,’ not a distribution. It exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster. Customers get standard clusters and use kubectl . The operator manages them through the NVKE API or the nvkectl CLI. NVKE uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API . It is written in Go and has no runtime dependency on NVKR. What does NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR) do? NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions . It produces executables, container images, Helm charts and node images for amd64 and arm64. ‘Recipes’ define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. Hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references. NVKR can also build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. How does the NVKE architecture work? The NVIDIA technical blog wa

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released two open-source projects, NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), as components of its DSX AI Factory Platform. Both projects are currently in public preview under the Apache 2.0 license. NVKE functions as a control plane for managed Kubernetes services, utilizing upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm, and Cluster API to allow users to run managed clusters on their own bare-metal GPU infrastructure. NVKR serves as the supporting build system, generating OS images, container images, Helm charts, and packages for both amd64 and arm64 architectures, while attaching SBOMs and provenance to OCI-referenced artifacts.

Technically, NVKE is written in Go and operates as a self-hosting factory for clusters, managed via a REST API or the nvkectl CLI. Deployment requires a minimum footprint of three CPU servers for the management cluster and three CPU servers per workload control plane, alongside a pool of GPU worker nodes; a local evaluation environment requires 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of RAM, and 100 GiB of disk space. While the platform is conformance-tested on Kubernetes 1.36 and holds Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Installer status, it currently lacks production-grade features, including management-plane upgrade or backup procedures, and defaults to unauthenticated HTTP on port 30080 post-installation.
takeaways: **Architecture:** NVKE is built on upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm, and Cluster API, and is designed to run on bare-metal GPU servers provisioned via NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo).
**Build System:** NVKR uses declarative definitions to produce validated software combinations, container images, and node images, ensuring artifacts are digest-pinned with signatures and SBOMs.

**Deployment Requirements:** Production-grade setups require three CPU servers for the management cluster and three per workload control plane, while local evaluation requires 6 CPUs, 12 GiB RAM, and 100 GiB disk.
**Security Status:** The current public preview release lacks authentication by default on the NVKE API and lacks established procedures for cluster backups or management-plane upgrades.
**Compatibility:** The platform supports both amd64 and arm64 architectures and is conformance-tested against Kubernetes 1.36.

title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
author: Wei Hou
contentSnippet: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

title: Sarvam Launches Sarvam Token Factory: Bringing India-Hosted Inference to 8 Open Models
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Sarvam has opened Sarvam Token Factory to everyone. Sarvam Token Factory is an inference platform from Sarvam that serves its own models and open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. Developers reach every model through one OpenAI-compatible API . For India-based teams, this means low-latency tokens without sending traffic to overseas clouds. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . Runs on: NVIDIA B200 clusters in India. Sarvam 105B now fits on 1 B200 per replica. On-premise deployment is offered to enterprises. Performance: Fastest first token from Mumbai on most tested cases, per Sarvam’s own measurements. Best: Kimi K3.1 Pro at 6,177 tokens/s per GPU vs 3,213 for InferenceX, at 70 tokens/s per user (1.9x). What is Sarvam Token Factory? It is a managed inference stack, not a single model. Sarvam first previewed it as Sarvam Inference at its Epoch event. The launch post lists 8 models: Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B. The docs split them into 2 groups. Pay-as-you-go models run on shared endpoints. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.8 27B, Clef and EmbeddingGemma 2 need Provisioned Throughput, enabled per organisation. How does it work? The stack has 3 layers around a shared cache: Control plane: a cache-aware router, admission control and a planner. Inference engine: separate GPU pools for prefill and decode. Cache: GPU memory plus a shared G3 store built on Mooncake. It builds on vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, Mooncake, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM and FlashInfer. An orchestrator agent proposes experiments, and an engineer approves each deployment. Caching drives most of the gains. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serves 450B+ tokens per day, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. On GLM 5.3, the planner cut prefill GPU-hours from 32.3 to 17.1 under the same replayed load. For Sarvam 105B, MXFP8 weights plus speculative decoding raised output throughput about 2.2x. That cut each replica from 2 B200s to 1. Sarvam says none of these changes reduced accuracy. summary.tldr:
Sarvam has launched the Sarvam Token Factory, a managed inference platform hosted on NVIDIA B200 GPU clusters located in India. The platform provides an OpenAI-compatible API for eight open-weight models, including Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and Gemma 4 31B. By localizing inference, the service aims to provide low-latency token generation for India-based teams, bypassing the need to route traffic through overseas cloud providers. The service is available via a pay-as-you-go model for shared endpoints, while high-demand models like DeepSeek V4 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro require Provisioned Throughput.

The platform's architecture utilizes a three-layer stack consisting of a control plane (router, admission control, and planner), an inference engine with separated GPU pools for prefill and decode, and a caching layer built on Mooncake. The stack integrates technologies including vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, and FlashInfer. Performance gains are primarily driven by cache-aware routing; for instance, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reportedly serves over 450 billion tokens daily with a 95.7% cache hit rate for prompt tokens. Sarvam 105B achieves a 2.2x throughput increase through the use of MXFP8 weights and speculative decoding, allowing the model to run on a single B200 GPU per replica instead of two.
takeaways: **Model Specifications:** Sarvam 105B features 105B total parameters, 9B active parameters, and a 128K context window.
**Performance Metrics:** Kimi K3.1 Pro achieved 6,177 tokens/s per GPU on the platform, compared to 3,213 tokens/s on InferenceX.
**Efficiency Gains:** The platform's planner reduced prefill GPU-hours for GLM 5.3 from 32.3 to 17.1 under identical replayed load conditions.
**Infrastructure:** The system utilizes a shared G3 store built on Mooncake and offers on-premise deployment options for enterprise clients.
**Optimization Techniques:** Sarvam utilizes MXFP8 quantization and speculative decoding to optimize memory footprint and throughput for its proprietary 105B model.

title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
author: Yifan Chang
contentSnippet: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.

title: Liquid AI Releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra: Omnimodal Decision Models That Top the AA Decision Index
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Liquid AI just released d1.2 and d1.2-ultra . A decision model does not write text. It returns calibrated probabilities over a fixed set of answers. The Liquid AI d1.2 decision model family now accepts text, images and audio. It also adds 5 new answer types. d1.2-ultra scores 75 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 , the top score among decision models on the index. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: Parameters not disclosed. Up to 65,536 input tokens per question , 128 questions per call. Runs on: Hosted Liquid API only. No weights yet; Liquid AI says it will open them “at some point”. Performance: d1.2-ultra 75 and d1.2 69 on the AA Decision Index v2.1. Best: 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 benchmarks (Liquid AI test). What is Liquid AI d1.2? d1.2 is a hosted decision model from Liquid AI that answers typed questions about text, images or audio in 1 call. It returns a probability per option and generates zero output tokens , so only input is billed. d1.2-ultra targets harder decisions. d1.2 is faster and costs less than half as much. The model IDs are d1.2 (default) and d1.2-ultra . Earlier d1 , d1.1 and d1-ultra are now deprecated and do not support audio or the new tasks. What are the 5 new tasks in d1.2? d1.2 adds 5 typed answers on the same endpoint and request format: Read a value ( text , number , date ): returns the value plus the characters it came from. It answers “not found” instead of guessing. Find every span ( spans ): returns each matching passage, such as names or emails, with its position. Locate objects ( box , boxes ): returns 1 rectangle, or 1 per instance with a count. Estimate a number ( number with range ): returns a best guess and a range, for example 12 within 10 to 14. Pick every option that applies ( choice with multiple ): returns each matching label with its own probability. How does audio input work? Audio can be the subject of a question, such as which language is spoken or whether a siren is audible. The question can also be spoken. The API takes 16-bit PCM WAV and counts 10 tokens per second of audio. On held-out ESC-50 and FLEURS (43 languages) recordings, both models answer 95% to 97% of questions correctly. summary.tldr:
Liquid AI has launched the d1.2 and d1.2-ultra decision models, a specialized class of AI that outputs calibrated probabilities over fixed answer sets rather than generating text. The d1.2-ultra model achieved a score of 75 on the Artificial Analysis (AA) Decision Index v2.1, currently the highest performance mark for decision models, while the standard d1.2 model scored 69. These models are omnimodal, accepting text, images, and audio inputs, and are designed to eliminate output token costs by returning only probability-based answers.

Technically, the models support up to 65,536 input tokens per question and handle up to 128 questions per API call. Audio processing is supported via 16-bit PCM WAV files, billed at a rate of 10 tokens per second of audio, with accuracy rates between 95% and 97% on ESC-50 and FLEURS benchmarks. The d1.2 family introduces five new task types: value extraction (text, number, date), span identification, object localization (bounding boxes), numerical estimation with confidence ranges, and multi-label classification. Liquid AI reports a 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 internal benchmarks.

Currently, the d1.2 models are available exclusively via the hosted Liquid API, with no public weight releases scheduled for the immediate future. The previous d1, d1.1, and d1-ultra models have been deprecated and do not support the new audio or task capabilities. Pricing for the standard d1.2 model is less than half that of the ultra variant, and the system is optimized for zero-output-token billing, meaning users are charged only for input processing.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** d1.2-ultra achieved a 75 score on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, while d1.2 achieved 69.
**Input Capacity:** Models support up to 65,536 input tokens per question and 128 questions per API call.
**Audio Processing:** Supports 16-bit PCM WAV files at a cost of 10 tokens per second, with 95-97% accuracy on ESC-50 and FLEURS datasets.
**Task Capabilities:** New functionality includes span extraction, object bounding boxes, numerical estimation with ranges, and multi-label choice selection.
**Deployment Status:** Models are hosted-only via Liquid API; weights are not currently public, and previous d1-series models are deprecated.

title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
author: Yijun Sun
contentSnippet: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading.

In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion.
takeaways: The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern.
Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency.
For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding.

We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.
