title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
author: Kibibi Moseley
contentSnippet: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.   Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26   Bringing Black Holes Into Focus Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process. With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit , black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes. By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull. Steering Fusion Simulations Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results. Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
author: Brett Murray
contentSnippet: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. From SC06 to SC26 NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack.   Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26   Honoring the Architects of Progress Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI: At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics , tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters , one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time. In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition , helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
author: Dan Ernst
contentSnippet: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.   Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26   Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. title: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
author: Jian Zhang
contentSnippet: With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails , you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended. When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns: Topics that block legitimate queries. A topic framed around a subject domain (Finance, Legal, Compensation) rather than the user’s intention can match queries semantically near that domain. This is a frequent failure mode. Topics that miss the requests they were written to catch. A definition built from keyword lists (“words like invest, portfolio, stock…”) misses phrasings that use other vocabulary and fires on unrelated inputs that happen to share those words. Examples that teach the wrong thing. Five paraphrases of one idea leave the topic’s boundaries unguarded, and examples that name specific countries, products, or companies pull those entities into the topic’s context. Topics that interfere with each other. Overlapping definitions compete for the same input, report matches inconsistently, and can together block inputs that neither would block alone. The rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t. The scenario: AnyCompany Bank’s customer assistant To ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things. Application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope. title: Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
author: Josh DeMuth
contentSnippet: With retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application. Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the new version when you’re ready. Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them. Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request. Why tenants need their own instructions Tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. title: Introducing explicit prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
author: Dustin Liu
contentSnippet: Many generative AI applications send the same long context with every request, and prompt caching avoids processing it again each time. That context can be a system prompt, reference documents, tool definitions, or the conversation so far. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency. Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both. The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save. As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models. For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. In this post, we use both modes with an open-weight model through the Chat Completions API and show how to read cache usage from each response. We then apply implicit caching to an OpenCode coding agent session on the same API and close with best practices. Prompt caching for open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from cache and processes only the rest. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, so the savings can grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input. See Amazon Bedrock pricing for the rates of each model. Supported modes depend on the model and the API. For each model’s caching modes, minimum prefix length, and how long entries stay cached, see Models at a glance . Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency.

Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both.
takeaways: The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save.
As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models.
For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching.

title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
author: MIT Technology Review Insights
contentSnippet: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. title: Risk-Aware Handover Management Approach for Non-Terrestrial Networks with the NTN-Connect Simulator
author: Mohammed Almekhlafi
contentSnippet: The continuous movement of low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites in non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) leads to frequent handovers, requiring joint optimization of visibility duration, transmit power, and user quality-of-service (QoS). This work address this issue by proposing a risk-aware handover management framework that minimizes transmit power and maximizes admitted users under per-satellite power budgets and user-rate chance constraints, while a preference score term penalizes short duration associations. We decompose the resulting mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) into an inner power allocation subproblem and an outer generalized assignment association subproblem. The inner subproblem reformulates the chance constraint into its deterministic counterpart using the value-at-risk (VaR) closed-form. The obtained transmit power allocation is then used in the association subproblem, which is solved optimally using an off-the-shelf solver. Finally, we employ the polynomial-complexity Hungarian algorithm to solve the relaxed assignment problem and enforce the per-satellite power budget using a knapsack algorithm. Simulations, using the proposed NTN-Connect simulator, on the OneWeb and Starlink constellations show that the proposed low-complexity solution achieves near-optimal performance and better performance compared to the risk-aware maximum stay (RA-MST) and risk-aware maximum received signal received power (RA-MRSRP) baselines. On the Starlink constellation, it increases the inter-handover interval (IHI) from $0.37$ to $1.47$~min, reducing the handover rate by $75\%$. At a maximum-IHI operating point, it reduces the total transmit power by 1.1 dBW (22\%) while increasing the admission rate from 97.4\% to 99.3\%.

title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
author: Yuhang He
contentSnippet: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

title: Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure . Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ‘. TL;DR Scale: Runs on Meta backend code with hundreds of millions of lines. The research paper analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Runs on: Meta’s internal infrastructure, overnight on spare capacity. Judge models in the paper: Llama3.3-70B, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4. Not publicly available. Performance: Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate at full scale (self-reported). Best: 74 privacy SEVs caught before landing in H1 2026; privacy SEV occurrence down 20%. Worst: The initial deployment confirmed only 8 of 41 reported catches (19.5%). Bottom line: Best: executable proof of a bug before merge. Worst: internal only, with self-reported numbers. What are Catching JiTTests? Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’ . Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. How does the JiTTests pipeline work? The production pipeline has 5 stages: Targeting: Runs overnight on spare capacity. It selects the previous day’s risky diffs, using a mechanism similar to Meta’s Diff Risk Score. Test generation: 2 diff-aware workflows produce candidate tests (explained below). LLM-as-Judge ensemble: Several LLMs score each failing test using the test code, failure trace, diff and inferred intent. RubFake: The Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment adds deterministic checks. Its rules flag patterns like reflection, broken mocks and not-implemented exceptions. title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
author: VicOne
contentSnippet: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A

summary.tldr:
Cybersecurity firm VicOne has identified 28 zero-day vulnerabilities within software and tools supporting the Physical AI and robotics ecosystem in under 48 hours. The research utilized AI-assisted discovery methods to scan projects maintained by major technology entities, including Google, NVIDIA, and Meta. While these findings are currently undergoing vendor and vulnerability-authority review, many lack assigned CVE tracking numbers, highlighting a significant gap in the security posture of the robotics supply chain.

These vulnerabilities are distributed across the entire robotics lifecycle, with 75% of the identified flaws concentrated in the development, training, simulation, and validation phases. The remaining findings impact deployment and runtime environments. The research warns that compromised components in these early stages could allow attackers to manipulate training data, alter pretrained models, or compromise the integrity of simulation environments, ultimately influencing the safety and operational instructions sent to physical robots.
takeaways: **Discovery Scope:** 28 zero-day vulnerabilities identified in less than two days using AI-assisted research tools.
**Affected Ecosystems:** Vulnerabilities impact software and tools developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta.
**Lifecycle Distribution:** 75% of the identified security flaws reside in the development, training, simulation, or validation stages of the robotics lifecycle.
**Operational Risk:** Compromised tools could allow attackers to inject malicious files into training systems or manipulate the models that govern robot behavior.

title: Alibaba Releases Qwen4-Max: 2.4T MoE, 71B Active, 1M Context
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen4-Max , the first model of its Qwen4 generation. Qwen4-Max is a proprietary sparse MoE model with a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B parameters active per token. It accepts text, images and video, and supports a 1M-token context window . Alibaba also cut API prices and reports a 62% drop in average cost per task. TL;DR Size: 2.4T backbone parameters, 71B active per token, plus 328B N-gram Embedding parameters. 1M context, 393K max output tokens. Runs on: Hosted only: QwenCloud API, Token Plan, Qwen Studio, QwenWork and Qoder. No open weights, so no self-hosting or quantized builds. Performance: A large jump over Qwen3.8-Max. Competitive with frontier models on agentic work, behind on hard coding and vision. Best: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agent work): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1, the next-best model. What is Qwen4-Max? Qwen4-Max is a multimodal MoE language model from Alibaba, built for long-horizon professional work. A Token Plan-only preview opened this month only . How does the Qwen4-Max architecture work? Qwen4 upgrades the sparse MoE design in 3 places: attention, residual connections and embeddings. GDN + Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA): Each QSA layer pairs with 3 Gated DeltaNet layers. These compress history into fixed-size states. QSA then uses a lightweight indexer to pick relevant context at micro-block granularity. This lowers attention and indexing cost on long sequences. Gated Residual (GR): 4 parallel residual branches use dynamic read and write gates. The aim is stronger information flow and better training stability. N-gram Embedding: 328B extra parameters provide lookups of local token patterns at layer 2. This adds capacity with little extra compute. Alibaba reports no loss spikes across the 2.4T-scale pre-training run. On in-house tests, Qwen4-Max-Base shows 5 to 13% lower bits per byte than Qwen3.8-Max-Base. It does this while activating 25% fewer parameters. How does Qwen4-Max perform on benchmarks? Alibaba’s comparison chart covers 16 benchmarks. Rivals are Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1. Several scores are cited from third-party leaderboards. None were independently reproduced at launch. Qwen4-Max ranks first on 4 of 16 benchmarks: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agents): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1 and 9.2 for Opus 5.5. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1: 46.7, versus 43.4 for Op

summary.tldr:
Alibaba’s Qwen team has launched Qwen4-Max, a proprietary multimodal sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model featuring a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B active parameters per token. The model supports a 1M-token context window with a 393K maximum output token limit. It is currently available exclusively via Alibaba’s QwenCloud API, Qwen Studio, QwenWork, and Qoder platforms, with no open-weight releases or self-hosting options provided. Alongside the launch, Alibaba announced a 62% reduction in average API cost per task.

Technically, Qwen4-Max introduces three architectural upgrades: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers paired with Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) for efficient long-sequence indexing, Gated Residual (GR) branches with dynamic read/write gates for training stability, and a 328B-parameter N-gram Embedding layer for local token pattern lookups. Alibaba reports that these optimizations allowed for a stable pre-training run without loss spikes, achieving 5–13% lower bits-per-byte compared to the Qwen3.8-Max-Base while activating 25% fewer parameters.

Performance claims indicate the model is highly competitive in agentic workflows, specifically leading on the HLAB-Vals-1.1 legal agent benchmark with a score of 21.3, significantly outperforming Kimi K3.1 (11.7) and Claude Opus 5.5 (9.2). While Alibaba cites top-tier performance across 16 benchmarks, including Agents’ Last Exam v1.1, the company notes that the model currently trails frontier competitors in hard coding and vision-specific tasks.
takeaways: **Architecture Specs:** 2.4T total parameters, 71B active parameters per token, and 328B N-gram Embedding parameters.
**Key Innovations:** Integration of Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) for micro-block indexing, and Gated Residual (GR) branches.
**Benchmark Performance:** Achieved a score of 21.3 on HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agent work) and 46.7 on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1.
**Deployment Model:** Strictly hosted via QwenCloud API and associated enterprise tools; no open weights or quantized builds available.
**Efficiency Metrics:** Reported 5–13% lower bits-per-byte than Qwen3.8-Max-Base with 25% fewer active parameters.

title: Hark Releases Handoff², a 2x Faster Computer-Use Agent for Hark Pro
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Hark has released Handoff² , the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app. The Hark Handoff 2 computer-use agent finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original, on average. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Runs on: Hark’s cloud. Each request gets a dedicated virtual computer. Users reach it from web, iOS and Android. No local or quantized option. Performance: 82% task completion on Hark’s 478-task internal benchmark, about 2x faster end to end than v1. Best: 93.8% on Hark’s internal alignment benchmark (v1: 90.3%). Worst: 82% browsing completion still trails Claude Opus 5.5 (max), by up to 5 points, in the same harness. Bottom line (best): Up to 3.8x faster flight booking and more than 5x faster long research. Bottom line (worst): Every Handoff² number is self-reported. No third-party score exists yet. What is Hark Handoff²? Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. How does Handoff² get 2x faster? Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. The model learned 3 habits: Batch actions, such as filling several form fields in 1 turn. Group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Reuse those composites as the task continues. Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal. The model outputs cursor and keyboard actions aimed at screen coordinates. Because savings stack per turn, gains grow on longer, browsing-heavy tasks. How fast is Handoff² compared with Handoff? Hark reports these speedups over v1 : Average: about 2x faster end to end. Fli

summary.tldr:
Hark has released Handoff², an updated computer-use agent integrated into the Hark Pro application, designed to execute web-based tasks by interacting with live browser interfaces rather than APIs. The agent achieves a 2x improvement in end-to-end task completion speed compared to its predecessor by utilizing a reinforcement learning (RL) training recipe that explicitly penalizes latency, wasted turns, and excessive thinking tokens. Since the initial preview in August and the October launch of Hark Pro, the platform has processed over 5.6 million browsing sessions and facilitated more than $20 million in transactions, including flight bookings, grocery orders, and job applications.

Technically, Handoff² operates on dedicated virtual computers—each equipped with its own browser, file system, and terminal—where the model outputs keyboard and cursor actions based on screen coordinates. The performance gains are driven by a new harness that allows the model to emit multiple actions per turn, enabling the agent to batch form-field entries and create reusable composite action patterns. On Hark’s internal 478-task benchmark, Handoff² achieved an 82% completion rate and a 93.8% alignment score, up from 90.3% in v1. Despite these gains, the agent still trails Claude Opus 5.5 by up to 5 percentage points in browsing completion tasks, and all performance metrics currently rely on self-reported internal data without third-party verification.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** Handoff² delivers a 2x average speed increase over v1, with specific task improvements reaching up to 3.8x for flight bookings and over 5x for long research tasks.

**Technical Architecture:** The agent utilizes a dedicated virtual computer per request and employs a training strategy that rewards batching form inputs and creating reusable composite action sequences.
**Benchmark Results:** The model achieved an 82% task completion rate on Hark’s internal 478-task suite and a 93.8% score on its internal alignment benchmark.
**Deployment Constraints:** Handoff² is exclusively available via Hark’s cloud infrastructure with no local or quantized deployment options; it is accessible via web, iOS, and Android interfaces.
**Competitive Context:** While faster than its predecessor, the agent’s 82% browsing completion rate remains up to 5 points lower than Claude Opus 5.5 in the same internal testing harness.

title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
author: Jun Wu
contentSnippet: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. We also report a negative result of practical value.

Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
author: Saptarshi Ghosh, Mohammad Saim, Tianyu Jiang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.

summary.tldr:
A study of 2,000 research papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR reveals a significant discrepancy between human and LLM-generated peer reviews. Researchers found that leading GPT and Claude models consistently derive 50% or more of their identified paper weaknesses from the appendix, regardless of whether the models are accessed via API, coding agents, or web interfaces. This behavior contrasts sharply with human reviewers, who source only 8.4% of their critiques from the appendix.

Technical analysis indicates that LLMs focus on fine-grained, non-central technical details buried in appendices, whereas human reviewers prioritize a paper's core contributions and presentation quality. The authors suggest this bias indicates that current LLM-based review tools may be misaligned with the priorities of the academic community. The research team has released their methodology and analysis code on GitHub to facilitate further investigation into AI-assisted peer review processes.
takeaways: **Dataset Scope:** The study analyzed 2,000 papers sourced from four major conferences: ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR.
**Appendix Bias:** LLMs attribute 50% or more of identified weaknesses to the appendix, compared to 8.4% for human reviewers.
**Critique Focus:** LLM critiques target granular technical details in appendices, while human critiques focus on core ideas and presentation.
**Consistency:** The observed bias remains consistent across API, coding-agent, and web-based LLM access methods.
**Resource Availability:** The research team published their analysis code at https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.

title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
author: Samarth Vinayaka
contentSnippet:
Authors: Samarth Vinayaka

Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.

Notes: 12 pages, 2 figures

summary.tldr:
In the paper 'When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors,' author Samarth Vinayaka investigates the performance degradation caused by hard-filtering memory systems in LLM agents. The research demonstrates that when memory resolvers incorrectly classify query-critical information as stale, the resulting 'false-drop' errors significantly impair downstream accuracy. Across three tested models, the study reveals that while hard-dropping stale facts yields performance gains of +0.186 to +0.230 under perfect resolution, the same mechanism results in losses of -0.176 to -0.181 when resolver reliability is low.

The study utilizes a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split to evaluate intervention strategies. A deployment-matched gate achieved an accuracy of 0.655, outperforming the 0.641 accuracy of a standard 'always hard-drop' policy, though it remained slightly below the 0.662 accuracy of a test-informed oracle. The findings indicate that false-drop errors are more detrimental to model performance than false-keep errors. The author concludes that global accuracy crossovers are insufficient as deployment thresholds because they are model- and task-specific, recommending instead that developers treat memory deletion as a cost-sensitive problem by validating false-drop risks on matched data or defaulting to label-free retention.
takeaways: **Performance Impact:** Hard-filtering stale facts shifts from a performance gain of +0.186–+0.230 to a loss of -0.176–-0.181 as resolver reliability decreases.
**Deployment Strategy:** A deployment-matched gate achieved 0.655 accuracy, compared to 0.641 for 'always hard-drop' and 0.662 for a test-informed oracle.
**Error Sensitivity:** False-drop errors (deleting critical information) cause significantly greater degradation to agent performance than false-keep errors (retaining stale information).
**Recommendation:** The author advises against using global accuracy crossovers as deployment thresholds, suggesting instead cost-sensitive validation or label-free retention.

title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
author: Shubhra Mittal, Gaurav Naresh Mittal
contentSnippet:
Authors: Shubhra Mittal , Gaurav Naresh Mittal

Abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Shubhra Mittal and Gaurav Naresh Mittal conducted a performance audit of four hallucination detection methods specifically for small, 4-bit quantized, on-device LLMs. The study evaluated Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, focusing on the practical constraints of single-GPU (Colab T4) deployment. The detectors tested include length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods: semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI.

The audit reveals that detector performance does not transfer across models; the ranking of detectors actually inverts between Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, evidenced by a Spearman rho of -0.80 and Kendall tau-b of -0.667. Furthermore, the study found that the low-cost lexical n-gram baseline performs statistically similarly to complex sampling-based consistency methods. The authors also identified a critical failure in the standard TruthfulQA-Generation evaluation pipeline, where the token-overlap-to-multiple-choice labeler yields near-chance AUROC scores (0.46–0.59), whereas the same detectors achieve 0.69–0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA.
takeaways: **Ranking Inversion:** Detector performance rankings are negatively correlated between Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, with a Spearman rho of -0.80.

**Baseline Efficiency:** Simple lexical n-gram baselines are statistically indistinguishable from resource-heavy sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on small, quantized models.
**Evaluation Methodology:** The standard TruthfulQA-Generation labeler is ineffective for small models, producing near-chance AUROC scores (0.46–0.59) compared to 0.69–0.89 on TriviaQA.
**Hardware Constraints:** The entire audit was conducted on a single Colab T4 GPU using 4-bit NF4 quantization, reflecting real-world on-device deployment limitations.

title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
author: Inish Melroy D Souza, Tom Jackson, Vitor Castro, Rebecca Higginson, Andrea Soltoggio
contentSnippet:
Authors: Inish Melroy D Souza , Tom Jackson , Vitor Castro , Rebecca Higginson , Andrea Soltoggio

Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.

summary.tldr:
LoRAWeaver, developed by Inish Melroy D Souza, Tom Jackson, Vitor Castro, Rebecca Higginson, and Andrea Soltoggio, introduces a training-free method for dynamic adapter routing in Large Language Models (LLMs). By treating adapter selection as a representation alignment problem within the adapter-output space, the method eliminates the need for retraining routers when new task-specific LoRA adapters are added to a system. This approach addresses the scalability bottleneck of managing growing pools of adapters in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) workflows.

The architecture functions by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against pre-defined task prototypes using cosine similarity. In empirical evaluations using LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B models on the 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark, LoRAWeaver outperformed existing training-free baselines in cross-task scenarios. The researchers report that the method achieves performance levels approaching those of trained retrieval encoders, despite requiring no additional learning phase for the routing mechanism itself. Ablation studies specifically validate the efficacy of directional alignment within the adapter-output space as the primary driver for selection accuracy.
takeaways: **Methodology:** LoRAWeaver utilizes cosine similarity to match query representations against task prototypes in the adapter-output space.
**Model Compatibility:** The technique was validated on LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B architectures.
**Benchmark Performance:** Testing was conducted across 48 tasks within the FLAN-v2 benchmark suite.
**Key Advantage:** The system is training-free, allowing for the addition of new adapters without the computational overhead of retraining a router.

title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
author: Animesh Agarwal, Meysam Ghaffari, Nina Fatehi, Carlos Morato
contentSnippet:
Authors: Animesh Agarwal , Meysam Ghaffari , Nina Fatehi , Carlos Morato

Abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.

Notes: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), Seoul, South Korea

summary.tldr:
Researchers Animesh Agarwal, Meysam Ghaffari, Nina Fatehi, and Carlos Morato introduced 'Tabular Population Priors' as a structured retrieval method for medication set prediction in electronic health records (EHR). Unlike current RAG systems that retrieve similar patient admissions for LLM inference, this approach utilizes a sparse condition-medication co-occurrence table derived from training data to rank medication class candidates. The method is designed to replace the patient retriever component in existing pipelines, such as PACERAG, providing a more task-aligned retrieval object for fixed-vocabulary structured prediction.

In testing on 1,004 held-out MIMIC-IV admissions, the drop-in replacement of the retriever improved F1 scores from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard scores from 0.218 to 0.237. Notably, these gains were achieved without increasing LLM call volume or requiring an inference-time patient index. A non-LLM top-k baseline achieved an F1 of 0.248, demonstrating the inherent predictive power of the population prior. The research, accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Structured Data for Health (SD4H), suggests that aggregate population statistics offer a more efficient and auditable alternative to patient-level nearest neighbor retrieval for clinical medication prediction.
takeaways: **Performance Gains:** Replacing the patient retriever in PACERAG with Tabular Population Priors improved F1 scores by 11.5% (0.303 to 0.338) and Jaccard scores by 8.7% (0.218 to 0.237).
**Methodology:** The approach uses a sparse condition-medication co-occurrence table estimated from training admissions to rank medication class candidates directly.
**Efficiency:** The system requires no additional LLM calls and eliminates the need for an inference-time patient index, improving both speed and auditability.
**Baseline Comparison:** A non-LLM top-k baseline achieved an F1 of 0.248, validating the predictive utility of the population prior before LLM integration.
**Dataset:** Benchmarking was conducted on 1,004 held-out admissions from the MIMIC-IV EHR dataset.

title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
author: Nathan Sheffield, Alek Westover, Lukas Finnveden, Alexa Pan, Julian Stastny, Ryan Greenblatt
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced 'NLS depth' (Natural-Language-Rooted depth), a new metric designed to quantify 'opaque serial depth'—the extent of unverbalized serial cognition within an AI model. Defined in arXiv:2611.17495v1, NLS depth measures the longest path through a model's computation that bypasses interpretable bottlenecks. The authors define NL-rooted nodes as those initialized from pre-training priors to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space remains restricted to that prior and is not re-interpreted by the model. This metric is designed to be computable pre-training based solely on architecture, training recipes, and deployment configurations, remaining invariant to post-training interventions like RLHF, distillation, or prompting.

Empirical analysis of open-weight models shows a strong correlation between NLS depth and layer count, with the metric exhibiting slow growth over recent years under standard transformer scaling. However, the authors warn that latent-reasoning architectures, such as full-bandwidth transformers, could significantly increase NLS depth. The paper provides a concrete worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B and advocates for the industry-wide adoption of NLS depth reporting as a necessary complement to direct Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitorability assessments to ensure AI transparency.
takeaways: **Metric Definition:** NLS depth measures the longest path in a model's computation that avoids interpretable, NL-rooted bottlenecks.
**Invariance:** The metric is designed to be insensitive to post-training techniques including prompting, distillation, and reinforcement learning.
**Scaling Trends:** NLS depth currently correlates strongly with layer count and has seen slow growth in standard transformer architectures.
**Risk Assessment:** The authors identify full-bandwidth transformers as a specific architectural class capable of significantly increasing opaque serial depth.
**Practical Application:** The paper includes a specific bounding calculation for the NLS depth of the Gemma3-1B model.

title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
author: Yavuz Yetim, Bor-Yiing Su, Zhe Wang, Arthur Liu, Pranav Sharma, Ying Wang, Randy Shuai, Luke Pfister, Ruichao Xiao, Bill Zhao, Zihao Liu, Liyuan Li, Jiangyuan Li, Gaoxiang Liu, Nathan Yan, Geonhwa Jeong, Jatin Chhugani, Elias Ellison, Uladzimir Pashkevich
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yavuz Yetim , Bor-Yiing Su , Zhe Wang , Arthur Liu , Pranav Sharma , Ying Wang , Randy Shuai , Luke Pfister , Ruichao Xiao , Bill Zhao , Zihao Liu , Liyuan Li , Jiangyuan Li , Gaoxiang Liu , Nathan Yan , Geonhwa Jeong , Jatin Chhugani , Elias Ellison , Uladzimir Pashkevich

Abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

summary.tldr:
A research team including authors from AMD and various engineering backgrounds has demonstrated the viability of Microscaling (MX) formats—specifically MXFP8 and MXFP6—for industrial-scale Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models. Unlike LLMs, which often tolerate 1% accuracy degradation, production R&R models require a strict Normalized Entropy (NE) margin of 0.01% relative to FP16/FP32 baselines. The study evaluates these formats on the AMD MI350X architecture, marking the first reported instance of native MXFP6 GEMM kernels that quantize both weights and activations while maintaining strict quality parity.

The researchers achieved significant performance gains by selectively applying MXFP6 to linear layers. Measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 reached 1.33–1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73–1.99x for MXFP6, with individual layers seeing up to 2.90x acceleration. When deployed in an end-to-end (E2E) inference pipeline, selective MXFP6 implementation yielded throughput improvements of 1.5–5.3% for Model A and 7.6–14.3% for Model B compared to existing FP8 configurations. The study concludes that MXFP8 serves as a robust alternative to row-wise FP8, allowing for flexible kernel selection based on GEMM shape.
takeaways: **Quality Constraint:** R&R models require a strict Normalized Entropy (NE) margin of 0.01% relative to FP16/FP32 baselines to be considered production-ready.
**Hardware Platform:** All empirical evaluations and kernel speedup measurements were conducted on the AMD MI350X architecture.
**GEMM Performance:** MXFP6 kernels achieved 1.73–1.99x speedups over FP16 across linear layers, with peak performance reaching 2.90x on specific individual layers.
**E2E Throughput:** Selective application of MXFP6 resulted in end-to-end inference throughput gains of 1.5–5.3% for Model A and 7.6–14.3% for Model B compared to FP8 baselines.
**Format Flexibility:** MXFP8 was validated as a viable alternative to row-wise FP8, offering comparable accuracy and allowing for optimized kernel selection based on specific GEMM shapes.

title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
author: Harrison C. Margolin
contentSnippet:
Authors: Harrison C. Margolin

Abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

Notes: 38 pages, 9 figures, 30 tables. Project page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Margolin Abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty.

We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
takeaways: In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing.
A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027).
Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion.
In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way.

title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
author: Ali Mohammadi Ruzbahani, Rezvan Abouzadeh
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.

title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
author: Kate M. O'Neill, Ian Whitehouse, Adam N. McCaughan, Ryan O'Loughlin, Sonia Buckley, Wolfgang Losert
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
author: Samuel Chen, Jiaru Bai, Austin Henry Cheng, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
author: Snehalkumar `Neil' S. Gaikwad, Dhruv Dixit, Bryen Alvarez, Pratik Patekar, Anika Sharma, Akshara Kolipaka, Paritosh Pandey
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
author: Aleksandr M. Shtraukh-Adamsky, Vladimir M. Adamsky, Irina G. Voloshina, Artemiy D. Spitsyn
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
author: Seyed Mahmoud Sajjadi Mohammadabadi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
